clinicalPearls: Presents with Whipple triad: symptoms of neuroglycopenia/adrenergic surge, documented hypoglycemia, and relief with glucose intake.
Neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, behavioral change, visual disturbance, seizure, coma) often dominate and can mimic a primary neuropsychiatric or seizure disorder.
Fasting-induced hypoglycemia is classic, but symptoms can also occur postprandially or with exertion in some patients.
Most insulinomas are small (<2 cm), solitary, benign, and confined to the pancreas; only a minority are malignant or multiple.
Multiple or recurrent insulinomas should raise suspicion for MEN1 syndrome, especially in younger patients or with a family history.
Weight gain is common because patients learn to eat frequently to avoid symptomatic hypoglycemia.
Diagnosis rests on a supervised fasting study demonstrating inappropriately elevated insulin and C-peptide during hypoglycemia, not just cross-sectional imaging.
Localization can be difficult since many tumors are very small; a negative scan does not exclude the diagnosis.
harrison.pathophysiology: Insulinoma is a neuroendocrine tumor arising from pancreatic beta cells that autonomously secretes insulin independent of glucose feedback regulation. This unregulated insulin release drives glucose into tissues and suppresses hepatic glucose output, producing hypoglycemia. The resulting fall in plasma glucose triggers counter-regulatory adrenergic activation and, when severe or prolonged, neuroglycopenia due to inadequate glucose delivery to the brain. Most tumors are sporadic and benign, but a subset occurs in the context of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1.
additionalDifferentials: Non-islet cell tumor hypoglycemia (IGF-2-secreting mesenchymal or epithelial tumors)
Autoimmune insulin (Hirata) syndrome or insulin receptor autoantibodies
Severe hepatic failure or sepsis-related hypoglycemia
nonInfectiousMimics: Factitious hypoglycemia from exogenous insulin or sulfonylureas
additionalInvestigations: 72-hour supervised fasting test — reference standard to document Whipple triad with paired glucose, insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin
Plasma insulin and C-peptide during hypoglycemia — inappropriately elevated levels confirm endogenous hyperinsulinemia
Sulfonylurea/meglitinide screen — excludes factitious hypoglycemia from oral secretagogues
Insulin antibody testing — helps exclude autoimmune insulin syndrome or exogenous insulin use
Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of pancreas — initial anatomic localization of tumor
Endoscopic ultrasound — high sensitivity for small intrapancreatic lesions not seen on cross-sectional imaging
Somatostatin-receptor or GLP-1 receptor based functional imaging — localizes lesion when anatomic imaging is negative
Genetic/family screening for MEN1 — indicated when tumors are multiple, recurrent, or early-onset
redFlags: Severe neuroglycopenia with seizure, coma, or altered mental status requiring urgent glucose correction
Recurrent or multifocal tumors suggesting MEN1 and need for broader endocrine screening
Imaging or biochemical features suggesting malignant insulinoma with metastatic potential
Hypoglycemia unresponsive to standard glucose repletion, suggesting an alternative or coexisting cause
Signs of another MEN1-associated tumor (parathyroid, pituitary) in a patient with insulinoma
pitfalls: Relying on a single random glucose or insulin level instead of a supervised fasting protocol, leading to missed or false diagnosis.
Failing to exclude factitious hypoglycemia (exogenous insulin/sulfonylurea) before pursuing extensive tumor imaging.
Assuming a negative CT/MRI excludes insulinoma, when small tumors frequently require endoscopic ultrasound or functional imaging for localization.
Overlooking the possibility of MEN1 in patients with multiple or recurrent insulinomas, delaying appropriate family and genetic evaluation.
harrison.prognosis: Most insulinomas are benign and solitary, and surgical resection is curative in the large majority of cases. Malignant or MEN1-associated multifocal disease carries a less favorable outlook and requires longer-term surveillance.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Hypoglycemia and Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors chapters
management: Cure most tumours with surgical resection — enucleation or partial pancreatectomy — after accurate preoperative localisation
Treat acute hypoglycaemia with oral or intravenous glucose and prevent it with frequent small carbohydrate-containing meals
Control hypoglycaemia medically before surgery or in unresectable disease with diazoxide, adding a somatostatin analogue such as octreotide or lanreotide where appropriate
For malignant or metastatic disease, use cytoreductive surgery, targeted agents such as everolimus or sunitinib, and peptide receptor radionuclide therapy
Screen for MEN1 in multifocal, recurrent, or young patients and offer genetic counselling and family testing when confirmed
Provide long-term surveillance for recurrence in malignant or MEN1-associated multifocal disease
